2. Materials and Methods
                                      This review incorporated elements of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic
                                 Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) [61]. It encom-
                                 passes the identification, selection, evaluation, and synthesis of available evidence in a
                                 narrative format.

                                 2.1. Information Sources
                                      The primary sources for the articles included the following online databases:
                                 PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. The comprehensive molec-
                                 ular biomarker database MarkerDB v2.0 (available at https://markerdb.ca/, accessed on
                                 3 March 2025) was searched for experimentally verified biological markers in humans [62].
 Life 2025, 15, 867                                                                                             5 of 31



                     2.2. Search Strategy
                         The search string included free terms such as “sports nutrition”, “allostasis”, “body
                     composition”, “allostatic load”, “allostatic overload”, and “physiological adaptation”. Each
                     term was combined with keywords such as long-term, chronic, acute, nutrition, exercise,
                     recovery, athletes, and biomarkers. The reference lists of the selected articles were also
                     manually searched for additional literature (snowballing).

                     2.3. Findings Presentation
                     7. Limitations and Future Directions
                         High-level sports already assess a wide array of biomarkers in athletes, along with
                     movement and sleep data, psychological measures, and practice, training, and performance
                     analytics, to monitor them. This is done to evaluate training progress, support recovery,
                     optimize performance, and prevent overtraining or RED-S. The proposed ALindex offers a
 Life 2025, 15, 867                                                                                           21 of 31

                     is no doubt that the proposed set of biomarkers requires further research to confirm their
                     validity and generate more accurate clinical recommendations for specific sports, sexes,
                     ages, and training phases. It needs to be noted that the available evidence indicates that nei-
                     ther the menstrual cycle [174–176] nor oral contraceptive use [177,178] significantly impacts
                     exercise adaptations or physical performance in women; however, individual monitoring
                     and sex-specific cut-offs may be warranted for athletes prioritizing elite performance.
                           The current information is primarily based on associations, underscoring the need
                     for more comprehensive studies that explore the longitudinal interactions between allo-
                     static overload (cacostasis) and sports performance. Additionally, as with other studies
                     in the field, there is a significant gap in terms of multilevel analyses, causal modeling,
                     and complexity-based approaches in the existing research [73]. Finally, more sensitive
                     laboratory methods are required to be included in sports practice to improve diagnosis and
                     reliability [179].

                     an evidence-based operational framework designed to enhance post-exercise recovery,
                     grounded in the allostasis paradigm. Under the allostasis–interoception paradigm, we
                     can consider syndromes such as overtraining, burnout, or RED-S as cacostasis or mani-
                     festations of allostatic overload in athletes. Despite its accuracy and robustness in clinical
                     settings for the assessment of morbidity and mortality, the allostatic load index (ALindex )
                     remains an underutilized tool that could effectively assess the exercise-induced cumulative
                     physiological burden in athletes. In this article, we cautiously propose an ALindex based
                     on 10 biomarkers tailored to physique competitors (with or without the use of PIEDs) and
                     elite athletes. To calculate the ALindex , each biomarker is equally weighted and summed,
                     resulting in an index ranging from 0 to 10 (a value of 1 is assigned if the biomarker exceeds

   "doi":"10.3390/life15060867",
   "abstract":"The paper updates the 4Rs sports nutrition framework for post-exercise recovery within the allostasis model. It offers practical recommendations for assessing allostatic load in athletes and proposes a cautious allostatic load index for physique competitors and elite athletes.",
   "tldr":"The 4Rs (Rehydrate, Refuel, Repair, Recuperate) remain a practical recovery framework, and the paper adds a proposed biomarker index to track cumulative physiological stress in elite and physique athletes. The index is a starting point that still needs validation before use in decisions.",
   "methods":"Review incorporating PRISMA-ScR elements, with searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science and Google Scholar using free-text terms on sports nutrition, allostasis and allostatic load, plus a biomarker database and manual reference-list searching. Results are presented in narrative form.",
   "findings":"The authors recommend replacing at least 150% of body mass lost, with sodium if faster replacement is needed. They cite about 1.2 g/kg per hour of carbohydrate for up to 4 hours after exercise for refuelling, and state that a ketogenic diet generally has neutral or negative effects on athletic performance compared with carbohydrate-rich diets. Creatine monohydrate may help recovery, while tart cherry, omega-3 fatty acids and dietary nitrate need further clinical research. The proposed ALindex sums 10 equally weighted biomarkers, each scored 0 or 1 against a cut-off, giving a 0 to 10 index; it is proposed but not tested in this paper.",
   "limitations":"The information is primarily associative, with little multilevel, causal or complexity-based analysis. The proposed biomarker set needs validation, and the authors note that sex-specific cut-offs and individual monitoring may be warranted for elite athletes. Blood draws must be standardised (rested, fasted, not after high-intensity work) for the index to be reliable.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use the 4Rs as a structure for post-training nutrition, with carbohydrate and protein refuelling matched to the time to the next session.    "athleteDev":"Performance Application: The framework supports post-exercise nutrition planning, and the ALindex may help organise biomarker and load data to spot cumulative stress in elite and physique athletes. The paper does not show that using the index improves performance.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The paper addresses recovery nutrition and allostatic load in athletes, and the authors mention injury recovery as part of the Recuperate step. It provides no return-to-sport criteria and no evidence on returning from injury."
 }
}

19	Introduction Younger age of first exposure (AFE) to American Football (football) is associated with later-life health problems
20	among former professional athletes in several studies; however, studies examining amateur (i.e., nonprofessional) athletes
21	are less clear.
22	Objective In a cohort of former amateur American Football players, this study assessed whether AFE to football was associ-
23	ated with: (1) psychiatric and neurobehavioral symptoms, (2) cognitive difficulties, (3) general health problems, (4) motor
24	symptoms, and (5) functional status.
25	Methods A cross-sectional survey study was conducted using the ResearchMatch platform. The key independent variable
26	was age of first exposure to football (AFE < 12 versus AFE ≥ 12). Main outcomes included depressive symptoms (Patient
27	Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety symptoms (Generalized Anxiety Disorders-7; GAD-7), cognitive difficulties (Brit-
28	ish Columbia Cognitive Complaints Inventory; BC-CCI), Neurobehavioral Symptom Inventory (NSI) score, and prevalence
29	of other health problems. Multivariable regressions were assessed for associations between AFE and outcome variables.
30	Results In total, 107 male participants with exposure to football (mean age: 60.6 ± 15.1 years) reported an average of
31	4.2 ± 2.7 years of exposure to football, with an average AFE of 11.7 ± 3.1 years. In multivariable analyses, AFE < 12 was
32	not a significant predictor of PHQ-9 (unstandardized beta, B: 0.51, standard error, SE: 1.25, p = 0.682), GAD-7 (B: 0.09,
33	SE: 0.95, p = 0.926), NSI (B: − 0.56, SE: 2.93, p = 0.850), or BC-CCI (B: − 0.65, SE: 0.77, p = 0.403). However, more prior
34	concussions were associated with worse PHQ-9 (B: 0.44, SE: 0.10, p < 0.001), GAD-7 (B: 0.33, SE: 0.07, p < 0.001), NSI
35	(B: 1.04, SE: 0.23, p < 0.001), and BC-CCI scores (B: 0.26, SE: 0.06, p < 0.001). AFE < 12 did not predict general health
36	problems or independent functional status.
37	Conclusions AFE to football was not associated with adverse psychiatric, cognitive, neurobehavioral, or general health
38	outcomes among young, former amateur American Football players. However, more lifetime concussions were associated
39	with adverse cognitive and psychiatric health outcomes. Future studies should examine similar outcomes in older cohorts
40	with more comorbidities to further minimize potential confounding between general health and lack of later-life symptoms.

 ORIGINAL RESEARCH ARTICLE



The Association Between Age of First Exposure to American
Football at a Young Age and Later‑Life Health Issues in Healthy,
Community‑Dwelling Adults
Grant H. Rigney1,2 · John E. Dugan2,3 · Anthony Bishay2,4,5 · Soren Jonzzon2,5 · Jacob Jo2,4,5,6 · Kristen L. Williams2,5 ·
Scott L. Zuckerman2,5 · Douglas P. Terry2,5

Accepted: 20 April 2025
© The Author(s) 2025


Abstract
Introduction Younger age of first exposure (AFE) to American Football (football) is associated with later-life health problems
among former professional athletes in several studies; however, studies examining amateur (i.e., nonprofessional) athletes
are less clear.
Objective In a cohort of former amateur American Football players, this study assessed whether AFE to football was associ-
ated with: (1) psychiatric and neurobehavioral symptoms, (2) cognitive difficulties, (3) general health problems, (4) motor
symptoms, and (5) functional status.
Methods A cross-sectional survey study was conducted using the ResearchMatch platform. The key independent variable
was age of first exposure to football (AFE < 12 versus AFE ≥ 12). Main outcomes included depressive symptoms (Patient
Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety symptoms (Generalized Anxiety Disorders-7; GAD-7), cognitive difficulties (Brit-
ish Columbia Cognitive Complaints Inventory; BC-CCI), Neurobehavioral Symptom Inventory (NSI) score, and prevalence
of other health problems. Multivariable regressions were assessed for associations between AFE and outcome variables.
Results In total, 107 male participants with exposure to football (mean age: 60.6 ± 15.1 years) reported an average of
4.2 ± 2.7 years of exposure to football, with an average AFE of 11.7 ± 3.1 years. In multivariable analyses, AFE < 12 was
not a significant predictor of PHQ-9 (unstandardized beta, B: 0.51, standard error, SE: 1.25, p = 0.682), GAD-7 (B: 0.09,
SE: 0.95, p = 0.926), NSI (B: − 0.56, SE: 2.93, p = 0.850), or BC-CCI (B: − 0.65, SE: 0.77, p = 0.403). However, more prior
concussions were associated with worse PHQ-9 (B: 0.44, SE: 0.10, p < 0.001), GAD-7 (B: 0.33, SE: 0.07, p < 0.001), NSI
(B: 1.04, SE: 0.23, p < 0.001), and BC-CCI scores (B: 0.26, SE: 0.06, p < 0.001). AFE < 12 did not predict general health
problems or independent functional status.
Conclusions AFE to football was not associated with adverse psychiatric, cognitive, neurobehavioral, or general health
outcomes among young, former amateur American Football players. However, more lifetime concussions were associated
with adverse cognitive and psychiatric health outcomes. Future studies should examine similar outcomes in older cohorts
with more comorbidities to further minimize potential confounding between general health and lack of later-life symptoms.

   "tldr":"In this survey of 107 former amateur players, starting football before age 12 was not linked to later depression, anxiety, cognitive complaints or general health problems. Lifetime concussion count was the factor linked to worse symptoms.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional online survey through ResearchMatch of men with football exposure, with age of first exposure dichotomised at under 12 versus 12 or older.  }
}

High school sport history came from public records and injury data from online databases.    "findings":"Of 2,556 players, about 64% were multisport athletes.
